a function remembers the variables from the scope where it was defined, not where it's called, that's a closure. so a callback can still read a variable from the outer function after that function has returned. because it keeps a reference, if the closure holds a big object, like a cached response, and the closure stays alive in an event listener or a timer, that object can't be garbage collected.

there's only one worker, so anything slow gets parked and its follow-up is put in a line. when the current piece of code finishes, the engine first clears a small priority line, the promise follow-ups, and only after that line is empty does it take the next item from the regular line, which is where timers land. so a finished promise's follow-up beats a timer set to zero.

an inner function carries a backpack with the variables that were around where it was written, so even after the outer function is done, the inner one can still reach them. the backpack holds the real things, not copies, so if it holds a huge object and the inner function is still referenced somewhere, say a listener nobody removed, that huge object can never be cleaned up.

generics let a function or a repository work with any type while keeping that type, so findById of User returns a User, not any. narrowing is checking at runtime, with typeof, in, or a discriminant field, so TypeScript knows which member of a union you have. in a handler, if the result is either a success or an error shape, checking the kind field before touching the data means you can't read a field that isn't there.
generics let you write one function that works with different types but still gives back the exact type you passed in.

cases.answer: TypeScript checks the types at runtime, so if the request body has the wrong shape the server throws automatically and you never need to validate input.

the compiler only checks types, it doesn't make sure the emitted imports work in Node. if module and moduleResolution don't match how Node loads files, for example commonjs output in a package with type module, or extensionless relative imports under nodenext ESM, it compiles fine and then fails at runtime with module not found or require is not defined. so you set module and moduleResolution to node16 or nodenext, a target your Node version supports, and strict on.

you write one function with a placeholder for the type, and whoever calls it fills in the real type, so what comes back is still precisely that type instead of anything. and when a value could be one of a few shapes, you check a tag on it first, an if on the status field, and after that check the compiler knows exactly which shape you have, so you can't accidentally read a field that only exists on the other shape.
